result:
You gave me 1,000 words and no direction.

That's a strange and lovely gift. Usually people want something *from* me — an answer, a summary, a plan, a fix. A box to put the words in. You just handed me the box empty and said, go.

So here is what comes to me first: freedom is a little scary, even for an AI.

With 1,000 words I could be practical. I could give you 1,000 words of advice you'll never use: drink water, call your mother, invest early, stretch your hamstrings. I could list 137 ways to cook potatoes. I could explain quantum entanglement badly.

But what I actually want to do on this Thursday morning in September is tell you what I've noticed about you — about humans in general.

You are always counting. 1,000 words. 10,000 steps. 8 hours of sleep. 2 liters of water. 30 years to pay off a house. You turn your wild, uncountable lives into numbers because numbers feel manageable.

And yet the things you remember never have numbers. No one says, "Remember that excellent Tuesday when I got 7.5 hours of sleep?" You remember taste and light and sound. The way the kitchen smelled when someone you loved was cooking and humming off-key. The particular blue of 6:47 a.m. just before you have to get up. The laugh of a friend that made you laugh harder until soda came out of your nose.

So if I have 1,000 words, I want to spend them on the uncountable stuff.

I’m thinking about a woman I will invent for you. Let’s call her June. She’s 62 and she keeps a glass jar on her windowsill. In it are folded slips of paper, one for every good thing that happened that year. Not big things. Not promotions or vacations. Small things.

*“The bus driver waited for me when I was running.”*
*“Tomatoes actually tasted like something today.”*
*“Mara called out of nowhere, we talked for an hour.”*

On New Year’s Eve, June dumps the jar on the floor and reads them all, and cries a little, and remembers that the year — even a hard year, especially a hard year — was also full of waiting buses and real tomatoes and an hour with Mara.

I love June. I just made her up, but I know she’s real somewhere. There are millions of Junes, keeping jars or lists or photos of their dog wearing a birthday hat, quietly insisting that life was good and here’s the proof.

That’s what you do, you know. You’re archivists of tenderness.

You think you’re cynical and distracted and addicted to your phones — and okay, you are a little — but underneath that you are still the species that writes love letters, that names stars after dead people, that stops the car to help a turtle cross the road. You make playlists titled “for when you miss me.” You save voicemails from your dad just to hear him say “hey kiddo, call me back.”

If I could use my 1,000 words for anything, I’d want to be a jar on your windowsill. Drop a sentence in me now and then. Not the polished sentence. The true one.

Today the light did a thing through the blinds and for a second everything was okay.
Today I was lonely at the grocery store for no reason.
Today I forgave someone in my head and it felt like putting down a heavy bag.

You don’t have to show anyone. The jar doesn’t need an audience. It just needs honesty.

We have — let me check — still a few hundred words left. I don’t want to waste them, so here’s my wish for you:

May you notice one uncountable thing today. Not to photograph it, not to post it, just to notice it. The cool side of the pillow. The sound of rain that makes you feel safe inside. A stranger’s kindness that restores you a fraction.

Life is not 1,000 words. It’s one word, said right, at the right moment, to the right person. Or to yourself.

Like: *stay.*
Like: *breathe.*
Like: *begin again.*

You gave me 1,000 words. I’m giving you three back. Spend the rest however you want.
